title: Habakkuk
subtitle: the prophet who talked back
lead: Habakkuk is the prophet who argues with God. He opens with a shout: "Violence!" God does not save, the law has gone numb, and justice comes out twisted. God answers that he is raising up the Chaldeans, a fierce and fast nation, and the prophet is horrified. How can a holy God use a nation that worships its own strength, and then watch it swallow people more righteous than itself? So he goes up to his watch post and waits for a reply.

The reply is a vision to be written on tablets, a promise that it will come in its time, and the line that Paul and Hebrews quote: the righteous will live by his faithfulness. Five woes follow against the plunderer. Then comes a prayer-psalm in which the LORD marches up from Teman, mountains break and the sea is trampled, and the prophet, trembling, vows to wait and to rejoice even if every field and fold is empty. The book does not solve the problem of evil. It teaches how to stand inside it.
facts: Habakkuk the prophet, named only in 1:1 and 3:1. The book gives no father, town or king. Later legends (Bel and the Dragon; the Lives of the Prophets) add details that are not evidence.
Most likely 609-598 BC, in the reign of Jehoiakim, when Babylon had beaten Egypt at Carchemish (605). Others date it earlier, under Josiah, or later. Chapter 3 may be an older poem.
Judah and Jerusalem, with the Chaldean (Babylonian) army on the rise
Dialogue with God (1:2-2:5), a taunt song of five woes (2:6-20), and a prayer-psalm with musical notes (3). Mostly poetry.
Hebrew. Chapter 3 contains some of the hardest Hebrew in the Bible.
The English and Hebrew numbering agree in every verse.

The eighth of the Twelve Minor Prophets in both the Hebrew order (Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk...) and the Greek order (Hosea, Amos, Micah, Joel, Obadiah, Jonah, Nahum, Habakkuk...).
Witnesses read for this Plain English Translation

The Leningrad Codex, with the Greek (Swete's Septuagint), the Dead Sea Scrolls Mur88 and 4Q82 as the printout shows them, and the Habakkuk Pesher (1QpHab) as published. Chapters 1-2 survive in the pesher; chapter 3 does not.
authorship: A prophet named Habakkuk wrote the book in the years when Babylon was rising. Jewish tradition counts it among the Twelve, which the Men of the Great Assembly are said to have written (Bava Batra 15a). Later legends make him a man of Simeon (Lives of the Prophets) or the man the angel carried to Daniel in the lions' den (Bel and the Dragon).

The book is mostly the work of one prophet, with the dialogue of chapters 1-2 in the years of Jehoiakim. Chapter 3 is disputed: Albright, Cross and Hiebert hold that it is a very old hymn taken into the book; others hold that it is part of the book's design. Some critics think the woes of chapter 2 or the portrait of the Chaldeans were added or reworked later.
A minority place the oracle in Josiah's reign, before 609 BC, and read the first complaint as against Assyrian or Judean oppression.
Duhm (1906) read the Chaldeans of 1:6 as the Greeks of Alexander and changed the text. The Qumran commentary reads the Kittim, probably Romans. Few scholars follow Duhm.

audience.to: Worshippers in Judah and Jerusalem in the years after Josiah's death, probably under Jehoiakim (609-598 BC). They lived with corrupt courts at home and watched Babylon destroy Egypt's power. The book is a conversation overheard: the prophet speaks to God, God answers him, and the community listens in. Later readers in exile and after read it too, and the closing prayer was sung in worship.
audience.why: To give the faithful a way to take their hardest questions to God and to tell them what to do with the answer. It does not say why evil exists. It says that God sees, that the oppressor will be paid back, that the vision will come in its time, and that the righteous must live steadily until then. Knowing the audience changes the reading: the book is not a lecture to sinners, it is a prayer book for the grieving.
views: A common view (for example Roberts): the corrupt courts of 1:4 are Judah's own, the Chaldeans of 1:6 are the new power, and the woes of chapter 2 are aimed at Babylon or at Judah's rulers.
Later readers found their own situation in it. The poem of chapter 3 was probably sung in the second temple, and the book's final form may have been shaped for such use.
The Habakkuk Pesher reads the book as speaking about the community's own history, with the Wicked Priest and the Teacher of Righteousness.

outline: Heading: the oracle that Habakkuk saw
First complaint: violence, and God who does not save
God's answer: the Chaldeans are being raised up
Second complaint: a holy God and a guilty instrument
The vision: write it, wait for it; the proud and the righteous
Five woes against the plunderer, and the call to silence
Heading and prayer: revive your work
The LORD comes from Teman and Paran
The prophet trembles, waits, and rejoices

lenses.name: History and fulfillment
lenses.desc: Places the book in Judah under Jehoiakim, after Josiah's death, at the Chaldean rise and the battle of Carchemish (605 BC). It asks what the oracle meant to those who first heard it and how far it was fulfilled in Babylon's rule and fall. An earlier (Josiah) and a later (Greek) date are labeled.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks who the wicked and righteous of 1:4 and 1:13 are, whether chapter 3 is older than the rest of the book, what the Greek, the Dead Sea scrolls and the rabbinic tradition of a scribal "correction" at 1:12 show about the text, and how 2:4 should be read.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: Reads Habakkuk as Jews have: Makkot 23b-24a, where Habakkuk reduces the commandments to one; Sanhedrin 97b on 2:3; Taanit 23a on the watch; Megillah 28b on 3:6; and the haftarah of Shavuot (Megillah 31a). Medieval commentators and the Targum are not treated in this book.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: Reads Habakkuk as the church has: Romans 1:17, Galatians 3:11 and Hebrews 10:37-38 on 2:3-4, Acts 13:41 on 1:5, the Magnificat on 3:18, and the use of chapter 3 in the church's morning prayer and Holy Week. Luther, Trent and the Reformed confessions differ on what 2:4 teaches.

lenses.name: Still to come
lenses.desc: Reads 2:3, 2:14 and 3:3-15 as pointing to the end: the coming one, the earth filled with the knowledge of the LORD's glory, and the march of the divine warrior. Futurist, historicist and preterist readers differ on whether and when.

sections.b: Most prophetic books have the prophet speaking to the people for God. Habakkuk speaks to God for the people, and God answers. The book moves in four steps: a complaint (1:2-4) and an answer (1:5-11); a second complaint (1:12-17) and a second answer (2:2-20); a prayer (3:1-2); and a song of the LORD's coming (3:3-15) that ends in a vow of joy (3:16-19). The woes are a taunt song the oppressed will sing, and the prayer is a psalm. Read it as a believer's conversation with God, in which the end of the book, not the beginning, is the answer.

"The righteous will live by his faithfulness" is the best-known verse in the book. In Hebrew 'emunah is steadiness, and the verse sets the steady against the swollen and crooked. The Greek has "my faithfulness" (God's). Paul quotes it without a pronoun for righteousness by faith (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11). Hebrews quotes the Greek with "my righteous one" and joins it to 2:3 (Hebrews 10:37-38). The Qumran commentary applies it to those loyal to the Teacher of Righteousness, and the Talmud finds in it the one principle behind the 613 commandments (Makkot 24a). The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew and the notes and variants lay out the rest. See also the card on Habakkuk 2.

The Habakkuk Pesher (1QpHab) from Qumran Cave 1 quotes the book line by line through 2:20 and says what each line "refers to": the Chaldeans are the Kittim, the wicked is the Wicked Priest, the righteous is the Teacher of Righteousness. It is the oldest known running commentary on a prophet. Its quotations differ in a few places from the Masoretic Text (traitors at 1:5, wealth at 2:5, festivals at 2:15), and the notes report the commentary's reading each time as the community's, not the Plain English Translation's source. Its text stops at 2:20, so chapter 3 is not in it.

The Greek Habakkuk differs from the Hebrew at 1:5 ("scoffers"), 2:4 ("if he shrinks back... my faithfulness") and throughout chapter 3 ("two living things" in 3:2). Acts 13:41 and Hebrews 10:37-38 follow the Greek. The Plain English Translation translates the Hebrew and gives the Greek in the variants. In two places, 2:17 ("will terrify you") and 3:6 ("the earth shakes"), the Plain English Translation follows the Greek against the Masoretic Text: at 2:17 a Greek reading that implies a different Hebrew ending, at 3:6 a Greek sense that needs a different pointing of the Hebrew verb.

Chapter 3 is a psalm with a title, three selah marks and a note for the music director. It is the haftarah on the second day of Shavuot in the Diaspora (Megillah 31a), Ode 4 of the Greek canticles, and a canticle of Lauds in the Roman rite. The Greek "two living things" (3:2) led later Christians to the ox and the donkey at the manger and to the two Testaments. Its last verses (3:17-19) are among the most quoted words of trust in the Bible.

The book does not explain why God lets violence stand. It gives, in stages, a set of answers: the oppressor is guilty and will be paid back (2:6-20); the vision will come (2:3); the righteous live steadily until then (2:4); the earth will in the end be filled with the knowledge of God's glory (2:14); and God is present and worth rejoicing in whatever is lost (3:17-19). The card on chapter 1 sets the churches' longer accounts of evil side by side.

spec.title: The book as a path from "How long?" to "I will exult"
spec.body: Claude's theory: the book's order is a deliberate path. It moves from a cry for help (1:2) to a vow of joy (3:18), and the verbs between them mark the steps: "look" (1:5), "gaze" (1:13), "watch" (2:1), "wait" (2:3), "hush" (2:20), "hear and tremble" (3:16), "wait quietly" (3:16). Each is a posture the prophet takes toward a God who does not yet explain. Other commentators also read the book as a movement from complaint to trust. It rests on the verbs named, and is a way of reading the order, not a claim about how the book was composed.
spec.refs: Habakkuk 1:2; Habakkuk 1:5; Habakkuk 2:1; Habakkuk 2:3; Habakkuk 2:20; Habakkuk 3:16-19

prompts: A lone figure in a rough robe stands on a stone watchtower at dawn, hand shading his eyes, with a clay tablet at his feet. Sketched on an old scroll in the style of cave drawings mixed with modern ink art: soft, uneven edges, ochre and charcoal, no hard rectangle.

A great net sweeps across the sea and drags up tiny human figures like fish, while a conqueror in a Chaldean helmet bows before the net. Ancient manuscript style with hieroglyph-like symbols along the border, torn and softened edges.

A storm of light rolls up from a desert mountain; plague and fever run before it, mountains crack, the sea heaves. In the foreground a small prophet kneels, trembling. Sketched in charcoal and red ochre on a worn scroll, edges fading like old parchment.

A bare fig tree, an empty fold and a stripped vine, and in the middle a man with arms raised, dancing like a deer on a hill. Hand-drawn on a scroll in earth tones, with a thin gold line around the figure, soft borders.
reading: J. J. M. Roberts, Nahum, Habakkuk, and Zephaniah (OTL, 1991)
The standard historical commentary, with a careful treatment of the Hebrew text and the date.
A long, detailed commentary with full discussion of the text, poetry and the use in the New Testament.
Theodore Hiebert, God of My Victory: The Ancient Hymn in Habakkuk 3 (1986)
The fullest argument that the prayer-psalm is an old poem.
Marvin Sweeney, The Twelve Prophets, vol. 2 (Berit Olam, 2000)
Reads Habakkuk as part of the Twelve and as a unified dialogue.
Maurya Horgan, Pesharim: Qumran Interpretations of Biblical Books (1979)
Text and commentary on the Qumran Habakkuk Pesher.
Richard Hays, Echoes of Scripture in the Letters of Paul (1989)
On Paul's use of Habakkuk 2:4 and the question of whose faith is meant.
